opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think this is one of the things that's actually quite different about robotics compared to, say, self-driving cars. With driving, you kind of have to get it right essentially everywhere before it's useful. The tolerance for error is really low, and you can't easily say, "Well, we'll just drive on this one street for now." But with manipulation, there's a huge range of tasks where a robot can be useful even if it's not perfect and even if it can only do a narrow set of things.

If you have a robot that can fold laundry, or sort packages, or load a dishwasher, that's already valuable. It doesn't need to do everything a person can do to justify being deployed. And crucially, many of these tasks are pretty forgiving. If the robot drops a shirt, it can pick it up and try again. A human can step in occasionally. So the cost of a mistake is often low, which means you can put systems out there before they're fully general.

The reason that matters so much is the flywheel. Once a robot is actually deployed doing something useful, it's collecting real experience: real objects, real environments, real failure modes. That data is exactly what you need to make the next version better and more general. So you start with a limited scope, the system does something people care about, it gathers data while doing it, and that data broadens what the model can handle. Then you expand to adjacent tasks, and the cycle continues.

I also think the foundation model approach makes this much more viable than it used to be. In the past, if you built a robot for one task, all that work basically stayed with that task. Now, with a general model trained across many tasks and many robots, the experience from folding laundry can actually help with, say, packing a box, because there's shared physical understanding underneath. So each narrow deployment doesn't just make that one application better. It contributes to the general capability. That's what makes "start small and grow" a real strategy instead of a series of dead ends.

r001.rationale: It contrasts driving’s low tolerance for error with manipulation tasks where a robot can drop an item, retry, and learn from real failure modes.

r002.rationale: The response does not characterize common sense as predicting plausible consequences before experiencing the mistake.

r003.rationale: It mentions general foundation models, but not LLMs or VLMs as a source of common-sense predictions for robotic learning.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the thing that's really appealing about the robotics side of this is that you don't have to solve everything at once. If you look at how language models got going, there was this kind of all-or-nothing flavor to it, where you need a model that can handle basically any text that someone throws at it before it's useful. With robots, it's a little different. You can put a robot into a setting where it only needs to do a fairly narrow set of things, and if it does those things reliably, that's already valuable. Think about a warehouse, or a kitchen in a restaurant, or a particular station in a factory. The scope of what the robot needs to handle in that setting is bounded, and you can get it to work well enough there to actually deploy it.

And the reason that matters is that once it's deployed, it's collecting data. It's experiencing the real world, it's encountering the edge cases, the weird situations that nobody anticipated in the lab. And that data is exactly what you need to make the next version of the model better and more general. So you get this flywheel where a narrow deployment feeds the data that lets you expand the scope, and the expanded scope lets you deploy in more places, which gets you more data, and so on.

I think the analogy that's maybe useful here is how self-driving cars progressed, except I'd argue manipulation is actually in a better position, because the cost of a mistake is usually much lower. If a robot drops a cup, that's unfortunate, but it's not the same as a car making a mistake at highway speed. So you can afford to deploy things that are a little bit imperfect and let them improve, which is really the thing that makes this incremental path viable.

And the other piece is that the foundation models themselves, the vision-language-action models that we and others have been building, they do generalize to some degree already. They have this prior from internet-scale pretraining about what objects are, what tasks mean, and so when you put them in a narrow setting, you're not starting from zero. You're starting from something that roughly understands the world, and you're specializing it. So the narrow deployment isn't really narrow in the capabilities of the underlying model, it's narrow in the scope of what you're asking it to be reliable at. And that's a much easier thing to grow out from.

r001.rationale: The response says a dropped cup is less costly than a driving mistake, but it does not identify mistakes as recoverable.

r002.rationale: The response does not characterize common sense as anticipating consequences before experiencing a mistake.

r003.rationale: It mentions pretrained foundation models and their rough understanding of objects and tasks, but not LLMs or VLMs providing common-sense predictions for robotic learning.

astra-6.text:
I think manipulation has a useful property, which is that you can constrain the task without necessarily eliminating its economic value. You can have a robot in a particular workstation, handling a particular set of objects, and doing one useful operation. It doesn't have to be able to do everything a person can do for that to be worth deploying.

And that deployment gives you a way to collect experience. You see the cases where it succeeds, the cases where it fails, and the cases where somebody has to intervene. If you can use that experience to improve the system, you can gradually expand the range of objects it handles or the operations it performs.

Now, that isn't automatic. If you build a very specialized machine, you might solve that one task without learning anything that helps with the next task. The interesting opportunity is to use a general learning system underneath a fairly narrow initial application. Then the application gives you a foothold, and the experience you collect can help you broaden what the robot can do.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is that you don’t have to solve every manipulation problem before you can do something useful. You can start with a fairly constrained setting, where the robot has to handle a particular class of objects or perform a particular task. And even within that setting, there’s enough variation that you have to learn something meaningful about how to interact with the world.

Then, as you deploy that system, you get more data. You encounter different objects, different arrangements, different ways that things can go wrong. If your system can learn from that experience, you can gradually expand the range of situations it handles.

Now, that expansion isn’t automatic. If you build a very specialized machine, you might end up having to redesign it for every new task. But if you use a general learning approach, the constrained task can be a starting point. It gives you a useful capability and a way to collect experience, and that experience can support the next capability.
